abstract: Background: Type-B aortic dissection requires separation of the true and false lumina in heterogeneous, anisotropic CTA. A topology term may reduce fragmentation, but its reproducibility must be tested under a fixed case split and independent native-grid evaluation. Methods: We used the public Graz type-B aortic dissection CTA collection (40 cases; CC BY 4.0) and froze a 28/6/6 case split for training, development, and held-out testing. A compact 2.5-D U-Net trained with cross-entropy plus multiclass Dice was compared with the identical model augmented by a fixed-weight (0.5) differentiable slice-level soft clDice term. Two training seeds were run for each arm. All 40 cases passed the NRRD audit; predictions for six held-out cases were restored to their native grids and scored with case-level 3-D voxel-grid Dice, voxel-grid morphological clDice, 6-connected component counts, physical-volume error, and 2,000-resample case-level paired bootstrap intervals. Results: With seed 20261007, topology-minus-baseline differences were -0.028 (95% CI -0.053 to -0.004) for true-lumen Dice, +0.032 (-0.006 to +0.096) for true-lumen voxel-grid clDice, +0.071 (+0.037 to +0.103) for false-lumen Dice, and +0.073 (+0.048 to +0.103) for false-lumen voxel-grid clDice. With seed 20261008, the corresponding differences were -0.040 (-0.065 to -0.018), +0.013 (-0.034 to +0.071), -0.099 (-0.187 to -0.004), and -0.058 (-0.124 to -0.001). Descriptive pooled means over 12 case rows per arm were true-lumen Dice 0.577 for topology versus 0.611 for baseline and false-lumen Dice 0.409 versus 0.422; these pooled rows are not independent cases. Conclusions: Under this fixed six-case test split, the corrected slice-level topology term did not produce a consistent benefit. True-lumen Dice was lower in both seeds, while false-lumen effects reversed direction between seeds; topology-clDice changes were small and/or interval-crossing. The benchmark supports an auditable failure-analysis workflow but does not support a general topology benefit, clinical use, external generalization, or a panvascular decision system.
